analysis.title: Market and Economic Update, November 2026: Resilient Growth Amid Market and Political Crosscurrents
key_insights: October was volatile for equities. The S&P 500 fell -0.9% and the Nasdaq -5.3%, while the Dow rose 1.7%. Year-to-date gains are 10.7% (S&P 500), 9.4% (Nasdaq) and 7.7% (Dow), per the report's ordering. Technology/AI stocks weighed on performance.

Long-term Treasury yields retreated from recent peaks. The 30-year closed October at 5.31% and the 10-year at 4.93%, back below 5%. The Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index returned 2.4% for the month.

Oil rose significantly in October on renewed Middle East tensions, with Brent at $118 a barrel and WTI just below $103. Higher oil complicates the inflation outlook and reinforces expectations that rates stay elevated.
The Fed held at 3.75%-4.00% in October, with two officials favoring a 25-basis point increase. The report calls it a 'hawkish hold'. The statement described activity as expanding at a strong pace.
September PCE prices rose 0.5% on the month and 3.6% from a year earlier. Core PCE was 3.1%. Inflation has exceeded the Fed's 2% target for 67 months.

Q3 GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized rate, the strongest quarterly pace in a year. Consumer spending grew 2.5% and business investment rose 3.3%. AI infrastructure spending contributed to investment, and the equipment imports it required weighed on net exports.

Trailing 12-month S&P 500 earnings growth is 32.2% against a historical average of 8.0%. Strong earnings have offset questions about AI spending and have moderated broad-market valuations compared with prior highs.

Several large technology companies reported pressure on free cash flow from infrastructure spending in October. Tech stocks are also sensitive to long-term rates because their cash flows lie far in the future.

Consumer sentiment (University of Michigan) fell to its second-lowest reading on record in October, while spending and GDP stayed resilient. The report attributes the gap to a K-shaped economy: households with financial assets benefit from rising markets, while those exposed to food, fuel and housing costs are strained.

The Nov. 3 midterms gave Democrats control of the House and Senate, creating divided government for the last two years of President Trump's term. Cost of living, tariffs, energy prices and housing affordability were major factors.

Divided government may reduce the odds of sweeping legislation. Budget and debt-ceiling negotiations require bipartisan agreement and could cause short-term volatility. Policy uncertainty on tariffs, taxes, debt and geopolitics may continue to weigh on sentiment.

Several local ballot measures addressed data-center construction, many favoring added restrictions over electricity demand, water use and local effects. Because AI infrastructure is a key contributor to business spending and growth, restrictions could affect individual companies and industries.

The report argues election outcomes have rarely determined long-term economic or market direction, and recommends a balanced portfolio and long-term focus rather than reacting broadly to election results.

Other October moves: VIX ended at 19.4 after a September low of 14.2, the Dollar Index fell to 101.9, and gold ended at $3,873 an ounce, described as a recent low. MSCI EAFE returned -0.8% and MSCI EM -8.1%.

sector_views.rationale: AI buildout is driving earnings and business investment across construction, power, equipment and semiconductors. Tech stocks fell in October on free cash flow pressure from infrastructure spending and sensitivity to long-term rates.

earnings_insights: S&P 500 trailing 12-month EPS growth was 32.2% (latest) against a historical average of 8.0%, per Clearnomics/LSEG data cited in the report.
Several large technology companies reported pressure on free cash flow from infrastructure spending during October earnings, despite earnings growth. No company names or figures are given.
